questions.prompt: DESIGN IT — auth and session design for a multi-user web product [mid] (tracer, docs/adr/0003-sessions-over-jwt.md). Scenario: a team issue tracker with a single-page app on its own origin, a REST API and a live WebSocket feed. About 50,000 users sign in through GitHub OAuth, stay signed in for up to 30 days, and an admin must be able to end a compromised session within seconds. Design how a signed-in user stays signed in across requests: the token and where it lives, what the server stores, the cookie settings and what each one defends, how the OAuth callback is protected, and what one authenticated request costs. Write it before you look, then tick the checkpoints you covered and add up the weights (suggested pass: 70% with every [w3] hit)

keyPoints.text: [w3] Chooses server-side sessions kept in the database the product already runs (Postgres), identified by an opaque random cookie, instead of a signed token held by the client.
[w3] Names revocation as the deciding requirement: because the server owns the session row, deleting it ends that session on the very next request.
keyPoints.quote: Instant revocation: deleting the row ends the session immediately.

keyPoints.text: [w2] The cookie value is an unguessable secret: 32 bytes from the crypto random generator, base64url-encoded.
[w2] Session tokens are treated like passwords at rest: the raw value exists only in the browser cookie, so someone who reads the sessions table cannot replay it as a login.

[w3] Each cookie flag defends something specific: httpOnly keeps page scripts (an XSS payload) from reading the token, SameSite=Lax keeps the browser from attaching it to cross-site POSTs and subrequests, and Secure in production keeps it off plain HTTP.
[w2] Expiry is enforced by the server on every lookup: a row past its expiry resolves to no user, whatever the browser still holds.

[w3] The OAuth callback is protected against login CSRF: the login route mints a random state, stores it in a short-lived httpOnly cookie and puts it in the authorize URL; the callback compares the two in constant time, so a forged callback without the matching cookie is rejected.
[w2] States the per-request cost: one indexed lookup by the token's digest on every authenticated request, which is cheap at this scale.
keyPoints.quote: Every authenticated request does one indexed session lookup by token hash.

questions.prompt: PRE-MORTEM — the same product at 10x (about 500,000 users, every page load and every socket checking the session), plus a named failure: a laptop with a live session is stolen and the admin deletes that user's sessions. What breaks first, and what in your design already handles it?

keyPoints.text: [w3] The first suspected hot spot is the session read on every request; the decision record names its own trigger to revisit, profiling that shows session reads as a bottleneck.
keyPoints.quote: session reads show up as a bottleneck in Sprint 13 profiling

keyPoints.text: [w3] The planned move is deliberately narrow: move only the session store to Redis and keep the same cookie and token model, so no client or cookie changes ship with it.
keyPoints.quote: session store (only) to Redis, keeping the same cookie/token model

keyPoints.text: [w2] For the stolen laptop the HTTP side needs no denylist: with the rows gone, the next request carrying that cookie finds no session and is treated as signed out.

[w3] The gap: the WebSocket authenticates once, at the upgrade, and keeps the resolved user on the socket, so deleting the session rows does not cut a feed that is already open; a long-lived connection has to be closed or re-authorized when its session is revoked.
[w2] A stolen JWT would have been worse here: it stays valid until it expires, whatever the admin does.
keyPoints.quote: a stolen or stale JWT is valid until it expires

keyPoints.text: [w2] Known hardening the project deferred and a 10x review should pick up: rotating the session on a privilege change and a per-session mutation rate limit.
[w1] The lookup refuses an expired row but never deletes it, so the sessions table only grows; at 10x a periodic purge of expired sessions belongs in the design.

questions.prompt: TRADE-OFF HANDBACK — defend sessions in Postgres against the alternatives the decision record names (stateless JWTs, Redis sessions), and say what the cookie and CORS posture buys for a single-page app on another origin. For each, say what you bought, what it cost, and which requirement put you on that side.

keyPoints.text: [w3] What a stateless JWT would have bought: no session store at all, and trivial horizontal scaling.
keyPoints.quote: No session store, trivially horizontally scalable.

keyPoints.text: [w3] What it costs: "log out everywhere" or "this session was compromised" needs a denylist, which brings back exactly the server-side state JWTs were meant to remove.
keyPoints.quote: requires a denylist that reintroduces the very server state JWTs

keyPoints.text: [w2] At this product's scale a session row is the simpler design and revocation comes with it for free.
keyPoints.quote: At our scale a session row is simpler and gives instant revocation for free.

keyPoints.text: [w2] Redis sessions would give faster lookups but add infrastructure before any need was measured; one datastore is simpler for now.
keyPoints.quote: adds infrastructure before we've measured a need for it

keyPoints.text: [w2] Logout is a server action, not just a client one: the logout route deletes the session row and clears the cookie.

[w2] Cross-origin SPA: CORS allows credentialed requests only from the web app's origin, so other sites cannot read authenticated responses; it is SameSite=Lax, not CORS, that keeps the cookie off their cross-site form posts.
[w1] Hold no secrets speculatively: the provider's access token is used to fetch the profile and then discarded, because a stored token is a liability with no current consumer.
